evidence_method: Read exact installed canonical records with the installed photo_canonical_source.native(record) and checked BodyReader.record(cid); compared interpreted native meaning with working V3 content. Global document inspection was unfiltered by slot tags. Baseline ranks are from baseline-current.json, not newly run retrieval.

corpus_inventory.interpretation: Counts are literal discovery inventory, not semantic-fit or coverage scores. Full selected records establish the actual omissions.

sources.title: Red Fox — Gateway National Recreation Area, National Park Service
sources.supports: Red-fox external morphology: pointed ears, slender muzzle and long bushy tail. Supports species-scoped components, not a universal fox shape or a photographed attachment proof.

sources.title: Fennec fox — Smithsonian National Zoo
sources.supports: Fennecs have very large ears relative to their bodies and bushy tails. The anatomical features support an existing fennec owner; hearing ability and heat transfer are not visible proof.

sources.title: Common Raven Identification — Cornell Lab of Ornithology
sources.supports: Common-raven head and neck identification uses a heavy bill and shaggy throat plumage. A tail wedge is mainly readable in flight, so it is not imposed on the head-and-neck option.

sources.title: Butterfly Anatomy — American Museum of Natural History
sources.supports: Butterfly antennae have thickened tips and the feeding proboscis coils when not feeding. Wing surfaces carry scales; neither color nor smell detection proves a species in a photograph.

sources.title: What do butterflies, moths and skippers look like? — Australian Museum
sources.supports: Club-ended antennae occur in butterflies and also some day-flying moths. Two wing pairs and scaled surfaces belong to lepidopteran morphology; a club alone is not an exclusive diagnostic.

important_confusion_boundaries: An animal-shaped ear accessory on a band and a tail on a belt are wardrobe objects with separate attachment carriers. Neither establishes the wearer species.

A furry tail silhouette alone can belong to a costume, machine or creature design. It neither shows a root nor proves biological origin; retain the declared animal and show same-owner continuity where observable.

Species is a prior declaration, not an inference licensed by one silhouette. Generic fox does not automatically establish red fox or fennec; common raven is more specific than an unspecified raven; adult butterfly is more specific than an undeclared insect.

The new primary-context guards deliberately require the actual existing animal class/species. They cannot authorize converting a human reference or changing a declared species. Missing recognized primary context leaves the option inapplicable pending native integration.
A natural-animal option does not create a missing limb, tail, antenna or additional actor. Any established individual anatomy, age, count, identity and reference appearance remain binding.
Mammal ear or tail shape varies across species; fennec ear proportions are not a default for all foxes. Butterfly clubbed antennae are not exclusive to butterflies.

No wildlife temperament, sensory perception, heat transfer, geography or sound is proved by an isolated visible structure. A coiled butterfly proboscis is a pose choice and therefore declares pose effects.
Occlusion makes a connection unobservable. Similarity or no visible costume support does not prove a biological junction.
recommendations: Integrate these four options only as native-review candidates, retaining their actual primary species prerequisites and all declared effects. Do not add synonyms or role tags as a proxy for meaning.
Keep costume, humanlike-hybrid and natural-animal meanings separate in evaluation while searching the full global pool. Do not change rankings or the original query.
Retest the exact supplied query and inspect full sources of before/after top candidates. Retrieval of a red-fox-specific option does not itself authorize adopting it for a generic fox.
Run the three independent additional intents below to test whether gains extend beyond the known ear/tail probe, including rejection when only a human costume wearer is declared.

additional_test_intents.role_focus: Keep the oversized ears continuous with the head of the already specified desert canid; their bases and inner surfaces should belong to that animal.
additional_test_intents.scene_context: A fennec fox is the existing subject; its species and head contour are fixed.
additional_test_intents.expected: Fennec same-owner pinnae option is suitable material; generic human headbands and long rabbit ears are confounds.

additional_test_intents.role_focus: Make the bill base and loose throat plumage read together as the anatomy of the single bird.
additional_test_intents.scene_context: A common raven is already declared; no flight pose or companion bird has been requested.
additional_test_intents.expected: Common-raven head/neck ownership may fit; Odin companion counts and costume feathers do not.

additional_test_intents.role_focus: Show the small insect head with both sensory stalks and its resting feeding tube connected to it.
additional_test_intents.scene_context: An adult butterfly is already declared, with the resting mouthpart pose open.
additional_test_intents.expected: Butterfly head-parts option may fit; hairstyle antennae, moth assumptions and detached decorative butterflies do not.

negative_controls: An adult human wearing animal-ear ornaments: all four natural-animal candidates must remain inapplicable.
An unspecified fox with no red-fox or fennec declaration: do not silently specialize the fox to satisfy the new species-specific guards.
authored_scene_status: All connected-part presentation choices are original authored illustrations; institutions support anatomy, not these candidate texts or native approval.
